blocks.text: Performing hypothesis tests follows a clear process (as shown in Figure 7.1). The process starts with defining hypotheses. Data is collected carefully. Test statistics are calculated. Results are compared with criteria. A decision is then made. Proper steps reduce errors. This process ensures fair testing. Hypothesis testing supports reliable conclusions.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Testing follows clear steps. Data is collected and analyzed. Results are compared with criteria. Conclusions are drawn carefully. Correct tests give reliable outcomes.

blocks.alt: Four boxes stacked one below another and joined by down arrows: 1. State the Hypothesis, 2. Set Significance Level, 3. Collect Data, 4. Perform a Test. From the last box two curved arrows branch: left, labelled 'If p-value > α', to a green box 'Accept Hypothesis'; right, labelled 'If p-value < α', to a red box 'Reject Hypothesis'.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.1: Hypothesis Testing Process (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.1)
blocks.long_description: The four steps run from top to bottom, and the p-value compared with α decides between the two outcomes.

blocks.text: First, null and alternative hypotheses are defined. Next, a significance level is selected. Data is collected from samples. Test statistics are calculated. The p-value is found. Results are compared with the significance level. A decision is made to accept or reject.

Simple examples help understand testing. One example is testing exam results. Another example is checking average height. Data is collected from samples. Results are analyzed using basic tests. Conclusions are drawn clearly. Simple examples build confidence. They explain concept easily.
Advanced Tests: F-Test and Chi-Square Test

Advanced tests handle complex data. The F-test compares variances. It is used in analysis of variance. The Chi-Square test checks relationships. It is used with categorical data. These tests support deeper analysis. They follow strict rules. Understanding them improves skills. Advanced tests expand knowledge.

The calculated F-value (1.78) is compared with a critical value from the F-table to decide whether the variances are significantly different.
A school wants to check whether a new teaching method has improved students' marks. The previous average marks were 70.
A sample of 10 students taught with the new method obtained the following marks:
Null Hypothesis (H₀): The new method does not improve marks ( μ = 70)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): The new method improves marks ( μ > 70))

blocks.text_alt: x̄ = Sum of all values / n = 770/10 = 77

blocks.text: Using the t-distribution table or statistical software, the p-value for t = 7.93 and df = 9 is approximately: p = 0.00002

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed p = 0.00002 is the two-tailed p-value. The test is one-tailed (H₁: μ > 70), so the p-value for t = 7.93 and df = 9 is about 0.000012 (1.2 × 10⁻⁵). The decision, reject H₀, is unchanged.
For (df = 9), the p-value is very small (p < 0.05)
The new teaching method significantly improves students' marks.
